"Bring round" is a phrasal verb. A phrasal verb is simply a verb paired with one or two small words (like up, down, in, out, round) that together create a new meaning — a meaning you often cannot guess just by looking at the individual words separately.

"Bring round" has four distinct meanings in English. Learning all four will make you fully fluent in how this phrase works.
Meaning 1: To Make Someone Regain Consciousness

This is the most literal and medical meaning. When a person has fainted, passed out, or lost consciousness, and someone takes action to wake them up and restore them to an aware state, that person brings them round.

Think of it this way: the unconscious person has mentally "gone away," and you are bringing them back round to the world of awareness.

Examples:

  • "She fainted in the heat, but the nurse brought her round with some cold water."
  • "The smell of ammonia was used to bring the boxer round after the knockout."
  • "The doctors worked for several minutes before they managed to bring him round."

Key point: The person doing the action (the nurse, the doctor) is doing something to someone else. If the unconscious person wakes up on their own, you would instead say they "came round" — the intransitive (no object) version of the same idea.
Meaning 2: To Persuade Someone to Change Their Opinion

This is probably the most common everyday meaning. When someone disagrees with you, opposes your idea, or is reluctant about something, and you gradually convince them through argument, patience, or persistence, you have brought them round.

The image here is of turning or rotating a person's viewpoint until it faces the same direction as yours — like physically rotating something to face you.

This meaning is very often followed by the word "to":

bring someone round to an idea / a view / a way of thinking

Examples:

  • "My father refused to let me study music, but I eventually brought him round."
  • "She was skeptical about the plan at first, but a good presentation brought her round."
  • "It took weeks, but we finally brought the committee round to our way of thinking."
  • "He wasn't keen on moving abroad, but she brought him round to the idea."

Key point: This meaning implies a process — it takes effort and usually time. You don't instantly "bring someone round"; you work at it. It also implies the person had genuine resistance before, not just mild uncertainty.
Meaning 3: To Bring Someone or Something to a Place (Usually Someone's Home)

This is the simplest and most straightforward meaning. It simply means to take or deliver a person or object to someone's location — usually a house or workplace — often as a visit or errand.

Examples:

  • "I'll bring round those documents you need tomorrow morning."
  • "She brought her new boyfriend round to meet the family."
  • "Can you bring the kids round on Saturday afternoon?"
  • "He said he'd bring round a bottle of wine for dinner."

Key point: This meaning is very common in British English in casual speech. Americans would more naturally say "bring over" or "bring by" in this same situation. The phrase implies going to someone's specific location rather than meeting them somewhere neutral.
Meaning 4: To Steer a Conversation Toward a Particular Topic

When someone carefully and deliberately guides a conversation in a specific direction — moving from whatever was being talked about toward a topic they want to reach — they bring the conversation round to that topic.

The image is of steering or turning a ship: you gradually change direction until you are headed where you want to go.

Examples:

  • "No matter what we talked about, he always managed to bring the conversation round to money."
  • "She skilfully brought the discussion round to the question of his resignation."
  • "After some small talk, he brought things round to the real reason for his visit."

Key point: This meaning often carries a subtle sense of cunning or calculation — the person is not just casually changing the subject, they are maneuvering toward something. The phrase almost always appears as "bring the conversation / discussion / subject round to..."
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

"Bring round" is a separable phrasal verb. This means the object (the person or thing being acted upon) can go either between the two words or after both words — but with one important rule.

✅ "We brought the patient round." — object after both words
✅ "We brought him round." — pronoun must go in the middle
❌ "We brought round him." — wrong with a pronoun

The rule is: if the object is a pronoun (him, her, them, it), it must go between "bring" and "round." If the object is a noun (the patient, my sister, the documents), it can go either in the middle or at the end.

Passive form:
You can also make it passive:

  • "She was finally brought round after several attempts." (Meaning 1 or 2)

Tenses work normally:

  • Present: "We are trying to bring him round."
  • Past: "She brought him round."
  • Perfect: "They have finally brought her round to the idea."
  • Future: "Do you think we can bring her round?"

"Bring round" is predominantly British English. American English speakers tend to use "bring around" for exactly the same four meanings. Both are correct; they just reflect regional preference. If you are learning British English, use "round." If you are learning American English, "around" will feel more natural.
A Quick Cheat Sheet of Synonyms (Without the Table)

For Meaning 1 (revive): revive, resuscitate, wake up, restore consciousness

For Meaning 2 (persuade): win over, convince, talk round, sway, convert, persuade

For Meaning 3 (deliver/visit): bring over, drop off, bring by

For Meaning 4 (steer conversation): steer toward, guide toward, navigate toward, turn to
One Final Tip: How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Context is everything. Ask yourself:

  • Is someone unconscious? → Meaning 1 (revive)
  • Is someone disagreeing or resisting? → Meaning 2 (persuade)
  • Is a physical object or person being taken somewhere? → Meaning 3 (deliver/visit)
  • Is a conversation or discussion being redirected? → Meaning 4 (steer)

These four situations are distinct enough that you will almost never confuse them once you know all four meanings.
